When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in the file itself. An older `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item.

`--print-questions > q.yaml` writes the questions, their descriptions, their policy flags and any assertion as YAML, and `onesie -f q.yaml` reads it back. The first line, `# yaml-language-server: $schema=URL`, lets an editor check the file against the JSON Schema that `onesie --print-schema` prints, and onesie reads it as a comment. Each top level key is a question id holding `ask` and optionally `pick` or `rate`, `yes_means` and `no_means`, `threshold`, `min_confidence` and `fallback`. A top level `assert` or `abstain_if` is the file's gate. An unknown key exits 2 rather than being ignored. An `--ask` beside `-f` adds a question, and reusing an id from the file needs `--replace`. `-f` also takes a request body, a file with a `questions` key such as `--print-request` writes. For one record, a body's own `state` is sent as it is, and stdin is then never read, so `--state` or `--state-file` beside it exits 2. A stream or `calibrate` sends each record as its state and warns that the body's state is ignored. Save a set the repository shares as `.onesie/questions/NAME.yaml`, after `mkdir -p .onesie/questions` since the redirect creates no directory, or one for every project under `questions` in the config dir that holds `profiles.json`, and `-f NAME` finds it. A value with no slash and no dot that is not a file in the working directory is a name, looked up in the nearest `.onesie/questions` at or above the working directory, then in the config dir, as `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json`. A name found nowhere, or with two files in one directory, exits 2 and names the directories. `onesie questions` lists every name with the file it resolves to.

A profile, stored with `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER`, holds a provider, its key and optionally a model. A run uses the profile `--profile NAME` or `ONESIE_PROFILE` names, or the default one, which `onesie profile use NAME` sets, and a profile's key and model beat the provider's variables. `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` runs without a profile on that provider. typesafe is the default provider and reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, plus `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` when they are set. openrouter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone, and never falls back to the TypeSafe key or those two variables. `jev-latest` works on both, but a pinned model id does not carry over: TypeSafe pins `jev-1.13.0`, OpenRouter pins `typesafe/jev-1.13`. berget reads `BERGET_API_KEY` alone and serves its own models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` names the rest. levanto reads `LEVANTO_API_KEY` alone and serves its Sage models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `sage-latest` alias. cloudflare reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, defaults to `typesafe/jev` through AI Gateway, which needs credits, and serves `clef`, `clef-flash` and `clef-omni`. It takes images but no Box or long context. `onesie profile show` names the profile, the provider and where the key lives.

`--profile` exits 2 beside `create`, `update`, `delete`, `use` and `list`, and beside `show` or `test` given a name. So does `--provider`, apart from `create` and `update`, where it is the profile's own provider. `show` and `test` with no name take both as a run does. A profile that does not exist exits 2, naming the profiles there are. A `--provider` that names a profile rather than a provider exits 2 with a hint to pass `--profile`.

A yes or no answer is a probability, or an object whose `value` is one. A pick or rate answer is a name, or an object with `value` and an optional `confidence`, which defaults to 1. With no `p`, the value's probability is the confidence, or twice what each other option or level gets when that is more, rounded up to four places, so it is never below the confidence. The others share the rest evenly in steps of 0.0001, the first of them taking one step more where it does not divide evenly. So the value is always the most likely, and the `p` printed replays. A rate's `score` is the level index averaged over `p`, rounded to four places, unless the entry gives one. A number whose text is a name is that name, so `4` rates `--rate 1,2,3,4,5`. A rate question from a request body takes its level index.

A mock run chooses its profile and resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a `--profile` that does not exist, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads `profiles.json` unless `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses the run. A mock run uses no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts no requests, tokens or attempts, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions answered, 0s`.

`--cache`, or `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, stores each successful response on disk and answers a repeated request from it. Without either, nothing is stored and nothing is read. `ONESIE_CACHE` takes the values the flag takes, such as `1`, `true`, `0` and `false`, and anything else exits 2 in every run and `calibrate`, `--mock` and `--print-request` included. `--cache=false` turns the cache off for one run under `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, so that run asks the API again.

On the `typesafe` provider, a model name that ends in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned, and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on any other provider, `typesafe/jev-1.13` on OpenRouter and `Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B` on Berget and `levanto-sage-v1.4` on Levanto included. An alias's answers expire after 24 hours, since the model behind it can move. `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` sets that lifetime as a duration, such as `90m` or `72h`, and `0` stops reading and storing answers for an alias. A negative or malformed value exits 2, in every run whether or not it uses the cache, in `onesie cache` and in `onesie cache clear`. A run's lifetime decides what it reads, not what it deletes: an expired answer is only a miss, which the next answer overwrites, and onesie deletes an alias's answer only once it is older than 24 hours, or than the run's own lifetime when that is longer. So a short lifetime in one run never deletes answers other runs still read. An answer stored at a time later than the clock reads is a miss too.

Its files are mode `600` in directories of mode `700`. `--cache` refuses a cache directory others can reach with exit 2, before any request. Windows carries no such modes, so the check is skipped there. onesie writes a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, so backup tools skip the cache, into a new cache directory and into an existing one that is empty or holds only what onesie writes. `--cache` refuses an existing directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` that holds anything else with exit 2, before any request, since a tag there would hide those files from backup tools, and entries stored without one could never be cleared. onesie counts, evicts and clears only its own entries and temporary files, and leaves anything else in a tagged directory alone. Writes are atomic, so parallel runs can share one cache.

`--stats` writes a one line summary to stderr, as in `6 records, 2 skipped by --resume, 1 cached, 3 requests, 3 questions asked, 412 in / 9 out tokens, model jev-latest, 4 attempts (1 retry: 429×1), 10s/attempt, 2.1s`. The records lead with every one the run read, and the counts after them are parts of that whole: those `--resume` skipped, the cache answered, deduplication shared, that failed, and the requests sent. A run of one record that became one request leads with `1 request` alone. The questions are those the requests asked, so a cache hit asks none. The tokens and the cost OpenRouter reports are summed over the requests, and the per attempt timeout is left out of a run that made no attempt.
Rounded rounds a number onesie computes itself to four places, so a gate, -o json and the table all see the same value rather than float noise.
Open opens the cache in dir, creating it with mode 700 and a CACHEDIR.TAG when it is missing. It refuses a directory others can reach, except on windows, and an untagged one holding foreign files.
Cost is the summed cost the provider reported, which only OpenRouter does, and nil otherwise.
A run that made no attempt waited on none, so a per attempt timeout would describe nothing.
A written p need not add up to 1, so the average is taken over what it holds.

At least twice what each other name takes keeps the value the strict mode, which replayed demands of a written p, since a rate reads its value from the first of equal modes. Counted in units of 0.0001, the value keeps its share exactly and the others split the rest, the first of them taking one unit more where it does not divide evenly.
Rounded up, so a confidence with more than four places never rises above the value's p. The small allowance keeps float noise, as in 0.6 times 10000, from rounding up a whole unit.
Cost writes a cost in dollars, rounded to the hundred millionth, which keeps a provider's float noise out of a line meant for people.

`--box` makes a question a box, answered with `left`, `top`, `right` and `bottom`, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner, and a `confidence`. It needs an image, as in Images below, and a provider that takes it, TypeSafe or OpenRouter, as on `typesafe/jev-1.14`. Cloudflare, Levanto and Berget refuse it before any request. On TypeSafe the model must serve it too: one that does not answers 400 `Invalid request`, and onesie then names `-m jev-preview`, which does. It takes no value and no `--desc`, `--threshold`, `--min-confidence` or `--fallback`. `-r` prints the four edges in that order, and `-o csv` writes them as four columns, `ID_left`, `ID_top`, `ID_right` and `ID_bottom`. A box always returns a box, even when the target is not there, so pair it with a yes or no question that asks whether it is.

An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters.

`-f` also takes a request body, as `--print-request` writes it, a positional question's body keyed `answer` included. For one record, a body that holds a `state` sends that state, and onesie then never reads stdin, since it cannot tell a pipe that holds text from one that is still open without waiting on it. `--state` or `--state-file` beside such a body exits 2, naming both. `-i request` refuses both flags the same way, since each body there holds its own state. A stream and `calibrate` read their records from stdin as usual and send each one as its state, so they use the body only for its questions, and say on stderr that its state is ignored. A body's `assets` are sent with it. When its state is ignored, an asset only that state named is dropped, and the warning counts it.

`--long-context`, or `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, raises the context limits to 262k tokens, which is slower and less accurate. It is written into a printed body as `long_context`, so a replay keeps it, and a `-f` body's `long_context: true` turns it on with no flag. A body's `false` does not turn off the flag or the variable. The flag wins over the variable, so `--long-context=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, as `--cache=false` does for the cache. It does not turn off a body's `long_context: true`, from `-f` or under `-i request`, since the body asks for it itself. Set that key to `false` in the body, or remove it, to run without it. `-i request` follows the same order for each body it replays, and under `--print-request` it writes `"long_context":true` into a body the flag or the variable turns it on for. A provider that takes no long context refuses the run with exit 2, and when `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT` turned it on, the message says so. It is experimental on TypeSafe's side.
The four place numbers the requirement compared, not the table's percents, so a miss by less than a percent still shows.
One no tied with the lowest yes, which counts half a pair of 22500.

Whole percents unless they would hide something: a share that is not none reading 0, one that is not all reading 100, or two different numbers reading the same. A four place share is exact at two places, so the search always ends.
From the four place value in whole hundredths of a percent, since 0.565 times 100 lands just under 56.5 in floating point and would round down.
Wilson returns hits of of as a share with its 95 percent Wilson score interval, each rounded to four places and never to 0 or 1 unless it is exactly that. A share of nothing is not Defined.
The variable is easy to forget once it is exported, so a refusal it caused says so.
A member named with the value it already has is a choice the file already holds, so it is noted rather than refused. Naming none is still a mistake.
A file that cannot be read is listed as it is, since -f reports why when it reaches it.
Resolved for --print-request too, which prints the model a body that names none is sent with.
--print-request prints the body as it would be sent, with exit 0 and no network. The same predicate decides this and the client above, so the two cannot disagree and leave a nil client.

A scan of a body json.Valid passed, rather than a decode, so the assets a body carries are walked past and never copied. Only the exact key counts, since encoding/json would match Model for model too and the API reads only the exact one.

For a yes or no question the report has one row per cut. A row flags a record when `value >= cut`, the same test `--threshold 0.8` and `--assert 'urgent.value >= 0.8'` apply, so the cut goes into the gate as written. `catches` is the share of labelled yes records flagged, `false alarms` the share of labelled no records flagged, and `right when flagged` the share of flagged records labelled yes. Each shows the count, the share and its 95 percent interval, and on a few records the interval is the part to read: `2/2 99% 34-99%` says little. `worst misses` lists by id the records answered furthest from their label, each with the start of its mapped text on one line. Read them: a wrong label is fixed in the data, and a real miss means the question needs rewording and another calibration. A pick or rate question reports its agreement, a row per name with `found`, the share of the records labelled with it that were picked as it, and `right when picked`, the share of the records picked as it that carry its label, a table of labelled against picked, and one row per confidence cut with the share it answers and their agreement, which is where a `--min-confidence` comes from. The cuts run from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, and `--cuts 0.5,0.7,0.9` names your own.

`--out FILE` writes the answers to a file instead of stdout, with a fingerprint in `FILE.onesie` beside it. The fingerprint covers the questions, the provider, the model, `--map`, `--id`, the input and output modes, the merge key, the policy flags, `--assert` and `--abstain-if`, and `--skip-blank` when a resume counts lines, which is without `--id` on any input but csv and tsv. So `-j`, `--timeout` and `--retries` can change between runs, and `--skip-blank` can change with `--id` or on csv or tsv input. `--resume` exits 2 when any of those changed, saying `the questions, flags or gate changed`, or when a non empty file has no fingerprint or one from another onesie version, and says to drop `--resume` to start over. With `--id` a resume skips every record whose id the file already answers, with no request, and asks the rest, including a record whose last line was an error. Each answer is appended as it arrives, so an interrupted run loses nothing. Only a run with both `--resume` and `--id` rewrites the file once it completes, in input order with the newest line per id, and keeps the answered ids the input no longer holds after the rest, so a cut short input never deletes an answer. `--prune` drops those instead. `--resume` on a missing or empty file starts fresh, so pass it on the first run too. Until the rewrite the file can hold a record twice and out of order. Only the id is compared, so a record whose content changed but whose id stayed the same keeps its old answer. A skipped record keeps its stored assertion outcome, so it still counts toward exit 1 or 7 and toward `--stats`, and under `--stop-on-assert` a skipped false assertion stops the run with nothing after it asked. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume without `--id` drops a trailing error line and asks its record again, since a run stopped by `--stop-on-error` writes nothing after it, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it came from a run without `--stop-on-error`, and the resume stops there before any request, with the code that run exited with, or with exit 2 for a csv or tsv row, which keeps only the failure's message. Pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. With `--id` the failed record is asked again and stops the run only if it fails again. `--unordered` is allowed since the rewrite restores the order. Raw output is refused in every resume, with `--resume needs output that keeps each record's outcome, which raw lines do not`, since a raw line keeps no id, failure or gate outcome. A second run into the same `--out` file exits 2 until the first ends. A device or a pipe, such as `/dev/stdout`, gets no fingerprint and no lock, and `--resume` refuses one. A file or a directory onesie cannot write exits 2 before any request. Without `--id`, `--resume` counts the complete lines instead, drops a line cut off mid write, skips that many input records, retries no failed one but a trailing error line under `--stop-on-error`, and refuses `--unordered`. A stored error line it skips still counts as a failed record, so the run exits 6 and `--stats` counts it as failed, under `-i request` too. A full resume by id: `onesie 'is this urgent' -i jsonl -j 8 --map '.body' --id '.id' --out answers.jsonl --resume < tickets.jsonl`.

`--print-questions > q.yaml` writes the questions, their descriptions, their policy flags and any assertion as YAML, and `onesie -f q.yaml` reads it back. The first line, `# yaml-language-server: $schema=URL`, lets an editor check the file against the JSON Schema that `onesie --print-schema` prints. Each top level key is a question id holding `ask` and optionally `pick` or `rate`, `yes_means` and `no_means`, `threshold`, `min_confidence` and `fallback`. A top level `assert` or `abstain_if` is the file's gate. An unknown key exits 2 rather than being ignored. An `--ask` beside `-f` adds a question, and reusing an id from the file needs `--replace`. `-f` also takes a request body, a file with a `questions` key such as `--print-request` writes. For one record, a body's own `state` is sent as it is, and stdin is then never read, so `--state` or `--state-file` beside it exits 2. A stream or `calibrate` sends each record as its state and warns that the body's state is ignored. Save a set the repository shares as `.onesie/questions/NAME.yaml`, after `mkdir -p .onesie/questions` since the redirect creates no directory, or one for every project under `questions` in the config dir that holds `profiles.json`, and `-f NAME` finds it. A value with no slash and no dot that is not a file in the working directory is a name, looked up in the nearest `.onesie/questions` at or above the working directory, then in the config dir, as `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json`. A name found nowhere, or with two files in one directory, exits 2 and names the directories. `onesie questions` lists every name with the file it resolves to.

`--cache`, or `ONESIE_CACHE=1` in the environment of every run, stores each successful response on disk and answers a repeated request from it, with no request and zero tokens. A change to the state, the questions, the model, the provider or the base URL asks again, while `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--assert` and the output flags do not. On the `typesafe` provider a model name ending in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on OpenRouter or Berget, so its answers expire after 24 hours, or after `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL`. `--cache=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, so that run asks the API again. Cached answers stay on disk until they expire, are evicted or `onesie cache clear` removes them.

A yes or no answer is a probability, or an object whose `value` is one. A pick or rate answer is a name, or an object with `value` and an optional `confidence`, which defaults to 1. With no `p`, onesie fills one in where the value is the most likely and the others share the rest evenly. A rate's `score` is the level index averaged over `p`, unless the entry gives one. A number whose text is a name is that name, so `4` rates `--rate 1,2,3,4,5`. A rate question from a request body takes its level index.
The cache, deduplication and `--resume` see the same image file as the same record.

`--print-request` writes onesie's request format: the System One body plus the settings that change the answer, each image as base64 under `assets`. `-i request` reads lines up to `max-request-line-bytes`, so a printed body replays. A printed body holding `long_context` is refused by TypeSafe if sent to it directly, rather than through `-i request`.
OpenRouter takes each image where its reference stands. An image named in several places is sent once per place, and counts toward the body size each time.
A cached run still needs a key, even though a hit sends nothing. Under `--cache`, the no key message says so.

An empty or whitespace only variable counts as unset. A flag that names a value, such as a file, a model or a profile, exits 2 on an empty or whitespace only one, so `--mock "$UNSET"` never reaches the API. `profile update` is the exception, where an empty value clears a member.

A key goes to the OS keychain under the service `onesie`: the macOS Keychain, the Secret Service on Linux, or the Windows Credential Manager. The item is named `PROFILE@HASH`, where the hash stands for the config dir, so two config dirs never share one item. The profile's `account` holds the name. A converted profile keeps its item name until `onesie profile update NAME --key`.

`-f VALUE` reads VALUE as a file when one exists at that path. Otherwise a bare name loads `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json` from the nearest `.onesie/questions`, then from `questions` in the config dir, and last takes a starter set built into onesie: `moderation`, `personal-data`, `prompt-injection` or `shell-safety`. A saved file wins over a built-in set of the same name, so a copy to edit is printed elsewhere first, as in `onesie -f shell-safety --print-questions > shell-safety.yaml`, then moved with `mv shell-safety.yaml .onesie/questions/`. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions` empties the file before onesie runs, and `-f` then finds that empty file ahead of the built-in set. `onesie questions` lists every name `-f` finds, with a built-in set shown as `built in` and an empty saved file marked `empty`, or `"empty":true` under `-o json`. A question file is refused with exit 2 when it uses a YAML alias or when it is larger than `max-question-file-bytes`, and every error in a file names its path. A file that holds no question, such as an empty one, `{}` or only comments, adds nothing beside `--ask`, and on its own it exits 2, naming the file. One that hides a built-in set always exits 2, naming how to reach the set.

`--print-schema` prints the JSON Schema for a question file. The first line `--print-questions` writes is `# yaml-language-server: $schema=URL`, which an editor running the YAML language server reads, such as VS Code with the Red Hat YAML extension, to check each key and value as you type. The URL names the release tag the binary was built from, and `main` for any other build. A JSON question file names the schema in a top level `"$schema"` key, which onesie accepts and ignores, so `$schema` is a reserved question id. The schema accepts any request body as it is.
CheckAll reports the first answer in result that does not fit its question, as Normalize would.
Unusable is a 200 response onesie could not use. It has kind response in a stream and exits 4 in a single shot run, since the same request would only get it again.
A cache others can read, or a directory that may not be onesie's, is something the user asked for and has to fix, so each ends the run. Any other failure only turns the cache off.
An entry that fails the answer checks would fail every run until it expires, so it is passed over and replaced by a fresh answer.
Ahead of the keychain and of New, so a base URL that carries a key is refused in onesie's words and nothing is sent.
The usage is read apart from the answers, so a 200 whose answers onesie cannot read still reports what it cost.
--print-request needs the resolution too, to print the model a body with none is sent with.
A resume is left to the flag rules, whose message names --resume as the flag with nothing to do.
Ahead of the request mode rules, so a flag both of them reject is reported against --list-models, which is the flag that made the mode meaningless.
Both ahead of the output and streaming rules, so a dry run is rejected before anything it would have written reaches stdout.
In a fixed order, so a command line with several offenders reports a predictable one rather than whichever check happened to be written first.

Guarded to --print-request, since --print-questions writes the assertion into the file it prints and so is the one dry run that carries it. A gate that only the file carries is ignored, so a gated file can be dry run as it stands.
Checked for every mode, since --merge applies to the non streaming ones too.

Also for every mode. The rule is rejected rather than clamped, and a typo in a shared alias is exactly as wrong outside a stream as inside one. Gated on jobsSet because jobs is an int and its zero value cannot be told from the flag being absent.
A resource hint rather than a semantic one, and it may reasonably come from a shared alias, so it warns and proceeds rather than failing.
Its own rule rather than the -o one, since run leaves Output empty for a bare -r.
The path that returns before a plan is built, so the rule has to sit above it.
Rejected before anything reaches stdout, which is the reason the rule lives in checkFlags rather than in the print path.
A passing case that warns is a rule firing where no rule was expected. A failing one is allowed to carry whatever the checks reached before the fatal error.
A second line of defence that never fires today. It goes false only if stripFlags stops dropping a value with its flag, or insertFlag stops leading with the mode flag.

No status arrived and the network did not fail, so the record never became a request, as with a line onesie could not read. Calling it transport would blame the network, and exit 5 where a fresh run exits 2.
KindTransport is a connection that failed or timed out.
Kind names what failed, so a consumer can tell a retry worth making from a record to fix.
ErrStaleAnswers matches every StaleAnswersError, so a caller tells a stale file apart without reading the message.
Open resolves and locks the answers file at config.Path and reads what a resume skips. When an error comes after the lock, the File comes back still locked for the caller to release.
Write appends to the file, opening it on the first write.
StaleAnswersError refuses a file whose fingerprint does not match the run. Sidecar is the file the fingerprint is kept in.
ResumeLedger reads the answers a resume by id skips. It is nil when the run does not resume by id.
In file order, so the reads move forward through the file.
Verdict is a stored line's outcome: rejected by the gate, abstained or failed.
StoredAt is where the file answers id, when it does.
Keep puts the line answering id in the order without asking it again.
Kept in its place and nothing more. The record is not asked, so it is neither pending nor skipped.
Wrote records where the line for slot was written.
Skipped counts the records a resume skipped.
Count adds one record with this verdict.
KeyInKeychain means the key went into the keychain item Account.
`--out` writes to a file with a fingerprint beside it, and a lock so two runs cannot share it.

`--resume` refuses with exit 2 when a change would alter what a record is asked or what its line holds: the questions or their policy flags, the provider, the model, the images, long context, `--mock`, the input or output format, `--map`, `--id`, `--merge-key`, `--assert` or `--abstain-if`. `--skip-blank` counts too when a resume counts lines, which is without `--id` on any input but csv and tsv. A file written by another onesie version is refused the same way. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.

Under `--stop-on-assert`, a skipped false assertion ends the run where a fresh run would stop. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume by line count whose last line is an error line drops that line, asks its record again and carries on. A run stopped by `--stop-on-error` leaves exactly that, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it was written without `--stop-on-error`, so the resume stops there before any request and exits with the failed record's own code, as a fresh run under `--stop-on-error` would. A csv or tsv row keeps only the message, so there it exits 2. Either way, pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. The same holds under `-i request`. With `--id` the failed record is asked again, and stops the run only if it fails again.

Deduplication covers repeats within one run, the cache covers repeats across runs, and `--resume` skips the ids an `--out` file already answers. A group of identical records asks the cache once, so a group whose first record hits counts one cached record and the rest deduplicated. A cached line in `--out` carries zero usage like any other hit. Turning the cache on or off never refuses a resume, so a file written with the cache resumes without it, and the other way round. `calibrate --cache` works too.

A request with an image waits up to 60 seconds per attempt, unless `--timeout` says otherwise. `onesie -V` lists it as `asset-attempt-timeout`, beside `attempt-timeout`. Lower `-j` for large images, since each record in flight holds its image bytes.

`show` never reads the keychain or prints a key. `key:` is `keychain` or `file`, with `, ends in XXXX` when the key has 16 characters or more, `env` and the key variable for a run without a profile, or `none`. A converted keychain key shows no ending until `onesie profile update NAME --key`. `chosen by:` is `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE`, `the default`, `--provider`, `ONESIE_PROVIDER` or `nothing`, and `not active` for a named profile a run would not use. `model:` and `base_url:` give the value a run would use, in the order a run picks it, then where it comes from. The model comes from `profile`, `env TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` or `the provider's default`, as in `model: jev-latest, the provider's default`. The base URL comes from `the profile's base_url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, `the profile's account_id`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `the provider's default`, the words a run's messages use. `base_url:` is `none` on cloudflare with no account, and a base URL a run would refuse exits 2 with the run's message. An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters.

A base URL that holds a user or a password, or any `@`, `?` or `#`, or that does not parse, exits 2 before any request, whether it comes from `--base-url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` or a profile, so a key never travels in a URL or reaches a message. So does one with no host or with a scheme other than http or https. The message names where the URL came from, `--base-url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` or `the profile's base_url`, and shows at most its scheme and host, as in `onesie: --base-url https:// names no host`. `profile create` and `profile update` refuse one too, and `profile show` refuses a profile that holds one. `--print-request` sends nothing and does not check it.
Resolved as a run resolves it, which checks a hand edited profiles.json and the provider's base URL variable too, since neither passed through create.
Result reads a missing answers object as an empty one, which is also the answer to a body that asks nothing, so only an empty result is read again to tell the two apart.

A Go toolchain, at the version `go.mod` names or newer, with `go install github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/cmd/onesie@latest`. It writes the binary to `$GOBIN`, or to `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` when that is unset, which is often not on PATH. If `command -v onesie` still finds nothing, have the user add that directory to PATH in their shell profile and open a new shell.

A profile, stored with `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER`, holds a provider, its key and optionally a model. A run picks its profile in the order [Choosing a profile](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#choosing-a-profile) gives, and a profile's key and model beat the provider's variables. `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` runs without a profile on that provider. typesafe is the default provider and reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, plus `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` when they are set. openrouter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone, and never falls back to the TypeSafe key or those two variables. `jev-latest` works on both, but a pinned model id does not carry over: TypeSafe pins `jev-1.13.0`, OpenRouter pins `typesafe/jev-1.13`. berget reads `BERGET_API_KEY` alone and serves its own models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` names the rest. levanto reads `LEVANTO_API_KEY` alone and serves its Sage models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `sage-latest` alias. cloudflare reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, defaults to `typesafe/jev` through AI Gateway, which needs credits, and serves `clef`, `clef-flash` and `clef-omni`. It takes images but no Box or long context. `onesie profile show` names the profile, the provider and where the key lives.

A run uses one profile, or none. [Choosing a profile][choosing] gives the order a run picks it in, [What a run uses][uses] where the key, the model and the base URL come from, and [profiles.json][file] where the file lives. No provider falls back to another's key.

A requirement reads `[lower|upper](ID.MEASURE) OP NUMBER [at CUT]`. `MEASURE` is `catches`, `false_alarms`, `right_when_flagged` or `auc` for a yes or no question, `agreement` for pick and rate, and `within_one` for rate. `OP` is `>=`, `>`, `<=` or `<`. `NUMBER` and `CUT` are fractions between 0 and 1, so `95` exits 2 with `write 0.95, not 95`.

A yes or no measure other than `auc` is read at one cut. `at CUT` names it, and `at abstain` takes it from the `-f` file's `abstain_if`. Without `at`, the file's `assert` gives it, when it compares the question as `ID.value < X` or `ID.value >= X`. A gate that compares the question with `>` or `<=`, through a function such as `max()`, through `in`, or at two different cuts gives none, and the requirement then needs `at`. A missing cut exits 2 before any request, naming the question.

A run `--stop-on-error` ends exits with the failed record's own code, as in [Exit codes](#exit-codes). A record that never became a request, such as a line onesie could not read or an empty state, has no code of its own, so it exits 6 as it does without the flag, and its error line is the only report.

A key the server refuses exits 3, on a run or on `test`. On a profile the message names `onesie profile update NAME --key`, and without one it names the provider's key variable. A run with no key and no profile for its provider names `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER`.
Answer is the normalized shape for one question. Absent fields are omitted, which is what makes a yes or no answer a bare value, not a mostly empty object.
A yes or no decision stays boolean whether it came from a threshold or from a fallback, so a consumer can branch on the JSON type without knowing which produced it.
ScoreYesNo scores yes or no answers, whose values lie in [0,1], against their labels. A record is flagged at a cut when its value is at or above the cut, and failed counts failed requests.
YesNoCase is one answered record of a yes or no question, with its label and the value answered. ID is nil when the run has no --id, and Line is the record's input line.
A labelled question keys the probabilities by its own labels and drops the legend, which is the opposite of the body case below.

options wires the tree through the public options where they exist, so the command tree resolves the config dir from the environment as it does in production. It turns the built in sets off, so a test sees only the files it names.
The ordered bytes the loader kept, not a Go map marshalled again, so the body reaches the wire in the order it was written.
Boolean is the parsed value for a yes or no question, where decision stays boolean.
BuiltIn is the name of the built in set, empty for a file.

List reports every name Find would resolve, the repository set first, then the config dir's, then the built in sets, each sorted by name. A name more than one place holds is listed once, from the first, since Find never reaches the others.

A onesie command in a code span or on a line of a fenced block. It may follow a pipe, a chain or env assignments, as in `ONESIE_MOCK=x onesie ...`, or sit inside `$(...)`. Its flags are checked against the help of the command they follow: the root before any subcommand, and after `onesie calibrate` or `onesie profile create`, that subcommand's own. A bare word where a subcommand can stand must be one. The command ends at a pipe, a chain, a redirection, a closing parenthesis or a lone `--`, so `onesie ... | jq -c --unbuffered` checks nothing of jq.
Order matters. The typed checks precede the general ones they would otherwise match, and silentError comes last so a real error joined to one keeps its code.
goccy reads a plain scalar such as 1e-7 as a string, where the loader reads a float, so a fixture holding one is left to its JSON twin.
WithLookupEnv replaces the environment lookup, so a test decides every variable a run reads.
Markdown reads an indented paragraph under a list item as prose, not as indented code.
RenderSkill renders the portable SKILL.md body for skill, writing the frontmatter fields accepts names. intro and sections are fragment contents in order, and the marker records source.
Set at link time by the ldflags in the Makefile and .goreleaser.yml.
Op is how a requirement compares its measured bound with its Threshold.
The command wrote the whole result to stdout, so a stderr line would repeat it.
A value alongside the error, because the engine writes every outcome. A nil value would print a blank line in place of the record.
pflag's Changed reports false for a name it does not know, with no error, so a name that has to survive a rename is spelled once here. A flag nothing passes to Changed needs no constant.
KeychainOption replaces one of NewKeychain's defaults, so a test needs no real keychain.
ReadFile returns the named file's content from disk, for Bump to edit.
Built only when the run makes a request, so -i request --print-request needs no key.
Ahead of the provider, since the schema is the same for every provider and a bad ONESIE_PROVIDER should not stand between an editor and it.

Detected here rather than inside Write, since the engine counts a failure from the evaluator's error and a rewrite inside Write would count as a success. A LineError gets kind input rather than the transport default from describe, so --stop-on-error reaches the row, and the line number comes along without a onesie prefix inside the JSON.
raw is deliberately left empty, which is what sends merge down the wrapper path rather than the splice. The object goes under state as raw JSON rather than a Go map, so its key order survives.
A stored failure a resume skipped fails the run as it failed the one that wrote it.

`--min-confidence` needs `--fallback`, which may be any value, so low confidence can route outside the options, as `human` does. Below the threshold `.decision` becomes the fallback text instead of the model's pick, and `.fallback` reads `low_confidence`, so a consumer routes on that field rather than trusting a low confidence guess. Above it `.decision` is the pick and `.fallback` is absent, which an assertion reads as the empty string. When the request fails, the record still carries `.decision` set to the fallback, with `.fallback` reading `error` and an `.error` beside it, and the exit code is the failure's. Under `-q` the record is not printed: a low confidence answer exits 1 and a confident one exits 0. In an assertion, `team.fallback == ""` holds only for a confident answer that arrived.

A yes or no question answers with how likely the yes is. `-r` prints only the answer. Without it, the table for a pick or a rate also shows the model's confidence and the probability of each option or level. Under `--threshold`, `-o table` and `-o markdown` write the decision as `yes` or `no` beside the probability.
The line on stderr reads `reading N records from FILE`, where a run that asks reads `asking N of M records`.

A file whose fingerprint does not match this run exits 2, naming the cause, such as the parts of the run that changed, or a fingerprint a newer onesie wrote. To regenerate the file, run again without `--offline` and `--resume`. The model and provider are part of the match, so pin both with `-m` and `--provider`.

Its files are mode `600` in directories of mode `700`. `--cache` refuses a cache directory others can reach with exit 2, before any request, apart from on Windows. onesie writes a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, so backup tools skip the cache. `--cache` refuses an existing directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` that holds anything else with exit 2, before any request, and names the file it found. The files a desktop leaves in a folder, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini` and any starting with `._`, do not count. onesie counts, evicts and clears only its own entries, and parallel runs can share one cache.

`show` never reads the keychain or prints a key. `key:` is `keychain` or `file`, with `, ends in XXXX` when the key has 16 characters or more, `env` and the key variable for a run without a profile, or `none`. A converted keychain key shows no ending until `onesie profile update NAME --key`. `chosen by:` is `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE`, `the default`, `--provider`, `ONESIE_PROVIDER` or `nothing`, and `not active` for a named profile a run would not use. `model:` and `base_url:` give the value a run would use, in the order a run picks it, then where it comes from. The model comes from `profile`, `env TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` or `the provider's default`, as in `model: jev-latest, the provider's default`. The base URL comes from `the profile's base_url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, `the profile's account_id`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `the provider's default`, the words a run's messages use. `base_url:` is `none` on cloudflare with no account, and a base URL a run would refuse exits 2 with the run's message. An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and prints the hint a run prints on stderr. It exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters, and after the report lines when `ONESIE_CACHE`, `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT` or `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` holds a value a run refuses.

A profile that does not exist exits 2, naming the profiles there are. A `--provider` that names a profile rather than a provider exits 2 with a hint to pass `--profile`. A `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE` or `profile show`, `test` or `use` name that is a provider and no profile exits 2 with a hint to pass `--provider`.

A file that does not parse or breaks a rule exits 2, naming the rule and the profile, never a key. A file cut short or holding a syntax error is `not valid JSON`, and valid JSON of another shape is `not a JSON object of profiles`. Every answer is checked against the question asked before it is printed, gated or cached, on a plain run, in a stream, under `-q` and `--assert`, in `calibrate` and when the cache is read. A yes or no value, each `p` and each `confidence` lies in [0,1], a pick names one of its options, a rate's `score` lies between 0 and its top level index, the keys of `p` are exactly the options, or the level indexes from 0 for a rate, and `p` adds up to 1 within 0.02. An answer of the wrong type fails too. Any of these exits 4 with `200 response could not be used:` and names the question and the value, as in `question 'urgent' answered 1.5, which lies outside [0,1]`. In a stream the record is an error line of kind `response`. Its tokens still count toward `--usage` and `--stats`, it is never stored in the cache, and it is not retried.

onesie adds the API path itself, such as `/v1/systemone`, so a base URL whose last segment is the first segment of that path, such as `/v1`, prints one warning naming where it came from, the segment and the URL questions go to. `--list-models` calls its own path, which the warning does not name. cloudflare's path is `/run`, so a cloudflare base URL ending in `/v1` does not warn. It is not refused, since a proxy may use that prefix.

onesie adds the API path itself, such as `/v1/systemone`, so a base URL that already ends in the start of that path, such as `/v1`, prints one warning naming where it came from, the segment and the URL questions go to. `--list-models` calls its own path, which the warning does not name. It is not refused, since a proxy may use that prefix. On cloudflare the path starts with `/run` instead, so a cloudflare base URL ending in `/v1` prints no warning, and one ending in `/run` does.
An empty base URL means none is stored.
MaxRetries is the ceiling on --retries. Each retry waits out a backoff, so a hundred bounds the wait at minutes rather than days.
Root is a command tree with the log of the failures that follow a run's failure, which cobra's one returned error has no room for. Command is the tree itself, for a caller to configure.
Run runs the tree once and returns its failure apart from the failures that followed it, for a caller that inspects the errors instead of exiting with them.

A mock run chooses its profile and resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a `--profile` that does not exist, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads `profiles.json` unless `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses the run. A test can point `ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR` at a fixture of its own, at mode `600`, whose profile holds a dummy `api_key`, since every profile must hold a key. A mock run uses no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts the attempts and retries as a live run does, with zero tokens and no cost, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions asked, 0 in / 0 out tokens, model jev-latest, 2 attempts, 10s/attempt, 0s`.
Started from the default, because a Go struct cannot tell an unset field from a zero one and the policy carries seven fields this run does not touch.
Held on the lines written, not the records answered, since under --unordered a record's line is written after its answer returns and would race the uncovered record's error.
The first record is held until the two behind it have been written, so input order and completion order disagree and only a run that writes on completion can put the first record last.
An interrupt can end the naming context before the engine's, so an --id it cut short ends the source and does not become a failed record.
The naming context is the first one the run derives, so cancelling only it as the first record is read opens the window a real interrupt can, where the engine's context is not yet cancelled.
Mocked says a mock file served the requests, so Requests counts the records it answered and the tokens are zero.
Record zero is the slowest, so a pipeline that wrote on completion rather than on position would put it last. Every other record has to wait for it.
Every goroutine is blocked once the dispatcher has stopped reading, so an engine that reads too far ahead has shown it by the time this returns.
Nothing is asserted in here. Logging to a test that has already failed its timeout panics, which would mask the hang with an unrelated failure.

Waiting for every worker to block makes this a real guard. Drain stops at the first write and would otherwise usually return before the workers fill the completion channel, so a missing select would go unnoticed.
WithEntry returns a copy of ctx whose request Transport answers from entry, as model answered it.
Two keys YAML tells apart, such as 0x1 and "1", send as one id, and the request would keep only the last of them.
Labelled stays false and Label stays empty. A body's criteria is a bare array with no names, which is the case the index keyed normalization exists for.
A rubric that names neither key replays as a bare question, as an absent or null one does.

Profiles live in `profiles.json`, in the config dir [profiles.json][file] names. The file is written at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in the file itself. A `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item.

`--profile` exits 2 beside `create`, `update`, `delete`, `use` and `list`, and beside `show` or `test` given a name. So does `--provider`, apart from `create` and `update`, where it is the profile's own provider. `show` and `test` with no name take both as a run does. Every `profile` command refuses `ONESIE_MOCK` and takes no `--mock`.
A notice onesie writes to stderr starts with `onesie: `, and a warning with `onesie: warning: `. The `--stats` summary and the `API key: ` prompt keep their own form.
The live key is in the environment of whoever runs this suite, and hiding all but the config dir proves the stored key is the one sent.
Compared as wire bodies, not as plans, because a body's levels have no labels and the file gives them index ones by design, so the two plans differ where the two requests must not.
